_note: Name-facts for the United States (FT-36, docs/PLAN_V0.8.md). See
American city names fall into a few repeating kinds, and saying which
kind a name is turns out to be the hook: a transplanted English or
Dutch name (Boston, Harlem), a Spanish saint (San Diego, San Antonio),
a native word the settlers kept (Chicago, Milwaukee), or a person
(Houston, Denver, Cleveland). Where the story is thin, the second fact
These ids are shared with usa-cities-east/-center/-west, so each
sentence is written once here and appears on all four maps.
seattle: Named for Chief Si'ahl of the Duwamish and Suquamish, who was friendly to the settlers; the city anglicised his name and he is buried across the sound from it.
Boeing, Microsoft, Amazon and Starbucks all started here.
portland: Decided by a coin toss in 1845: two founders wanted Boston and Portland after their home towns, and the Maine man won two throws out of three.
The losing penny survives and is on display in the city's historical society.
minneapolis: Half Dakota, half Greek: mni is water in Dakota, polis is city in Greek — the water city.
It has thirteen lakes inside the city limits, which is what the name was pointing at.
milwaukee: From an Algonquian word usually read as "good land" or "gathering place by the river".
Germans arriving after 1848 made it the beer capital of America — Pabst, Schlitz and Miller were all brewed here.
buffalo: Probably a mangled French beau fleuve, "beautiful river" — there were never any buffalo here.
The Erie Canal ended at its harbour, which is why it grew, and the St Lawrence Seaway bypassing it is why it stopped.
detroit: French détroit, "the strait" — the narrow water between Lake Erie and Lake St Clair that it guards.
Ford's moving assembly line started here in 1913 and cut the time to build a car from twelve hours to ninety minutes.
boston: Named for Boston in Lincolnshire, which is itself worn down from "Botolph's stone".
Its street plan follows cow paths and colonial shorelines, which is why it is the least grid-like big city in the country.
chicago: From shikaakwa, the Miami-Illinois word for the wild garlic that grew in the marshes here.
After the fire of 1871 it rebuilt with the first steel-framed skyscraper, and it reversed its river in 1900 so the sewage flowed away from the lake.
providence: Roger Williams, thrown out of Massachusetts for arguing that church and state should be separate, named it for "God's merciful providence" in guiding him there.
The colony he founded was the first to guarantee freedom of religion.
cleveland: Named for Moses Cleaveland, who surveyed it in 1796; a newspaper is said to have dropped the first a to fit its masthead.
Its river caught fire in 1969 — oil slick and debris — and the outrage helped produce the Clean Water Act.
bridgeport: Literally what it was: the port at the bridge over the Pequonnock.
P. T. Barnum was its mayor, and he built the circus's winter quarters here.
new-york: New Amsterdam until the English took it in 1664 and renamed it for the Duke of York.
Dutch names survive all over it: Brooklyn was Breukelen, Harlem was Haarlem, and the Bronx was the farm of Jonas Bronck.
pittsburgh: For William Pitt, British prime minister, named by the general who took the fort in 1758.
It keeps the -h that most American -burgs lost, after a twenty-year fight with the federal board that had spelled it Pittsburg.
columbus: For Christopher Columbus, chosen in 1812 when naming things after him was a young republic's way of claiming a founding story.
It is the Ohio one — there are Columbuses in sixteen other states, which is why this map has to say Ohio.
philadelphia: Greek for "brotherly love" — philos and adelphos — the name William Penn gave his Quaker colony's capital.
Penn laid it out on a grid with five squares in 1682, a century before anyone else in America thought to plan a city.
indianapolis: "Indiana" plus the Greek polis, coined in 1821 for a capital that did not exist yet.
Built on a site chosen for being the middle of the state, with no river worth using — one of the few big American cities not founded on navigable water.
denver: For James Denver, governor of Kansas Territory — the founders were flattering a man who had already resigned without knowing it.
The Mile High City, exactly: one step on the Capitol's west stairs is 5,280 feet above sea level.
baltimore: For Lord Baltimore, the Irish title of the family that founded Maryland; Baltimore itself is baile an tí mhóir, "town of the big house".
The bombardment of its Fort McHenry in 1814 is what Francis Scott Key was watching when he wrote the national anthem.
cincinnati: For the Society of the Cincinnati, Revolutionary officers who named themselves after Cincinnatus, the Roman who left his plough to save Rome and then went back to it.
It was called Losantiville for two years first, a made-up word meaning "town opposite the mouth of the Licking".
kansas-city: Named for the Kansa people, whose name is usually read as "people of the south wind".
There are two of them either side of the state line, and this is the bigger, in Missouri.
washington-d-c: George Washington chose the site but never called it after himself; Congress did that, and the District of Columbia is a Latin flourish for the same Columbus.
It is in no state on purpose: the founders did not want the capital beholden to one.
st-louis: For Louis IX of France, the crusading king made a saint — the city was French before it was American, and named for the patron of the king who then ruled it.
Its Gateway Arch is the tallest monument in the country, marking where the westward expansion set off.
sacramento: For the Santísimo Sacramento — the Blessed Sacrament — the name a Spanish explorer gave the river in 1808.
The Gold Rush started 60 km away at Sutter's Mill, and the city grew as the place the miners bought their shovels.
oakland: For the coast live oaks that covered the hills when it was founded in 1852.
Gertrude Stein grew up here and wrote the line everyone quotes against it: "there is no there there" — she meant her childhood home was gone.
san-francisco: For St Francis of Assisi, via the Spanish mission founded in 1776.
It went from about 1,000 people to 25,000 in a year when gold was found in 1848, and ships were abandoned in the bay by crews who ran for the hills.
san-jose: For St Joseph — the first Spanish civil town in California, founded 1777, before either San Francisco or Los Angeles had a village.
Now the biggest city in the Bay Area and the capital of Silicon Valley, which has no official boundaries at all.
virginia-beach: The plainest name on this map: the beach in Virginia, which is itself named for Elizabeth I, the virgin queen.
Its 56 km of seafront are in the record books as the longest pleasure beach in the world.
norfolk: For Norfolk in England — the "north folk" of East Anglia, as Suffolk were the south.
It has the largest naval base on earth, and the deep harbour is why the city is there at all.
las-vegas: Spanish for "the meadows" — there were springs and grass here, which is why a desert road stopped at this spot.
The springs ran dry in 1962; the city that grew on them now draws its water from the Colorado.
raleigh: For Sir Walter Raleigh, who sent the first English colonists to this coast in the 1580s and never set foot in America himself.
Like Indianapolis it was built to be a capital, chosen in 1792 for sitting near the middle of the state.
memphis: For the ancient Egyptian capital on the Nile — the founders were naming a city on a great river and reached for the grandest precedent they knew.
Sun Studio here recorded Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash and Jerry Lee Lewis, and Stax made the city the home of Southern soul.
san-bernardino: For St Bernardino of Siena, named by Spanish missionaries who crossed the pass on his feast day in 1810.
Route 66's original end ran through it, and the first McDonald's opened here in 1940.
los-angeles: Short for El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles — the town of Our Lady the Queen of the Angels, founded 1781.
It annexed its way to size: the map is full of independent cities it grew around rather than swallowed.
long-beach: Named in 1888 for the obvious: a long, flat beach, which the developers were selling.
Its port and Los Angeles's share one harbour and together handle about a third of everything imported into the country.
atlanta: A railway invention: the end of the Western and Atlantic line, feminised into Atlanta.
Sherman burned it in 1864, which is why almost nothing in the centre predates the Civil War.
irvine: For James Irvine, a Gold Rush merchant who bought a 400 km² ranch; the city was built on it in 1971 to a single plan.
One of the few large American cities that is entirely master-planned, village by village.
birmingham: For Birmingham in England, because both were built on iron — the founders were declaring an ambition in 1871.
It is the only place in the world with coal, iron ore and limestone, the three things steel needs, all within a few kilometres.
phoenix: Named by a settler who saw the canals of a vanished people and said a new city would rise from their ashes — the Hohokam had irrigated this valley for a thousand years and gone.
The modern canals follow the Hohokam lines, and the city is the hottest big one in the country.
mesa: Spanish for "table" — the flat-topped plateau the town was laid out on in 1878.
Bigger than Atlanta, Miami or St Louis, and almost nobody outside Arizona has heard of it.
dallas: Nobody is sure which Dallas: most likely George Dallas, vice-president in the 1840s, but the founder never wrote it down.
It has no natural reason to be there — no port, no pass, no mine — and grew because railways crossed at that spot.
fort-worth: An actual fort, built in 1849 and named for General William Worth of the Mexican War.
It calls itself "where the West begins", and the cattle drives up the Chisholm Trail are why.
san-diego: For San Diego de Alcalá, named on his feast day in 1602 — and the site of the first Spanish mission in California, in 1769.
Its bay is the best natural harbour on the coast, which is why the Pacific Fleet lives there.
austin: For Stephen F. Austin, who brought the first American settlers into what was then Mexican Texas.
The state capital, and the only big Texan city people describe as green and hilly — it sits on the edge of the Hill Country.
houston: For Sam Houston, who won Texas its independence at San Jacinto and then served as president of the Republic.
It has no zoning code, which is why a refinery, a cathedral and a taquería can share a block.
san-antonio: For St Anthony of Padua, named on his feast day in 1691 by a Spanish expedition camped by the river.
The Alamo was one of its five Spanish missions before it was a battlefield.
orlando: Probably for a soldier named Orlando Reeves who died here in 1835, though the records are thin enough that the town may have invented him.
Disney bought 110 km² of swamp through shell companies in the 1960s so nobody would raise the price.
tampa: A Calusa word recorded by the Spanish, meaning something like "sticks of fire" — possibly for the lightning, which is the worst in the country here.
Cuban cigar makers built Ybor City here in the 1880s, and José Martí planned the Cuban revolution from its rolling floors.
west-palm-beach: West of Palm Beach, which is named for coconut palms that grew from a Spanish ship wrecked in 1878 with 20,000 coconuts aboard.
Henry Flagler built it as the place his hotel's staff lived, across the water from the guests.
fort-lauderdale: Forts built in the Second Seminole War, named for Major William Lauderdale who commanded the men who built them.
It has 300 km of canals, which is why it is called the Venice of America.
miami: From Mayaimi, the name of a lake and the people beside it — a Native word, not a Spanish one, despite the city's Spanish present.
It was incorporated in 1896 by 344 voters, a third of them Black Bahamians, and it is the only major American city founded by a woman — Julia Tuttle.
